influenza A viruses and Sars-Coronaviruses are able to interfere with the induction of IFN-stimulated genes (ISG) through different mechanisms.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the molecular mechanisms of viral evasion and host defence, with a particular focus on the interferon (IFN) response.
the mechanisms of host defense and the evasion thereof by pathogens.
the molecular mechanisms by which influenza A virus and SARS-CoV evade innate immune responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

influenza A virus, and also the SARS-CoV, are able to inhibit the IFN response by multiple mechanisms, which may be virus specific, and may vary depending on the virus strain, cell type, IFN subtype and IFN concentration, or even the IFN signaling pathway.
the IFN response to influenza and coronaviruses is complex and involves multiple layers of regulation.
influenza virus and coronavirus infections are associated with a significant decrease in the induction of IFIT1, IFIT3 and OAS2.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the influenza A virus and SARS-CoV-2 are able to modulate host antiviral innate responses in different ways.
the influenza A virus (IAV) and SARS-CoV-2, two important respiratory pathogens, can both evade the host innate immune system.
the pathogenic influenza virus (PR8) is a potent interferon inducer but the virus also has the ability to modulate interferon stimulated gene (ISG) induction.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interferon response is not a monolithic system that can be turned on and off by one mechanism.
influenza A virus and SARS-CoV can both inhibit the induction of IFN-stimulated genes (ISGs) in infected cells, but they do so by distinct mechanisms.
there are multiple ways that these viruses modulate the interferon response, which may be a key component of their ability to cause severe disease.
